---
title: "Observational units"
---

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

## The original third rule

The original definition from the 2014 *Tidy Data* paper is:

1. Each variable forms a column
2. Each observation forms a row
3. Each **type of observational unit** forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you're observing,
for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit.
The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

## The tidy Billboard data, again

Here's the tidy Billboard data from Lecture 1's
[Tidy data](/lecture-01/02-tidy-data.qmd) section again.

```{r}
billboard_tidy <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
billboard_tidy
```

## Problem 4: multiple observational units

Our tidy Billboard table still mixes two kinds of things.
The song information (year, artist, track, time)
is repeated on every row, for every week the song was on the chart.
We can split it into two tables that share an `id` column.

```{r}
song <- billboard_tidy |>
  distinct(artist, track, year, time) |>
  mutate(id = row_number(), .before = 1)
song

rank <- billboard_tidy |>
  left_join(song, by = c("artist", "track", "year", "time")) |>
  select(id, week, date, rank)
rank
```

## Join them back together

The `id` column links the two tables,
so we can always join them back together when an analysis needs both.

```{r}
rank |>
  left_join(song, by = "id")
```

## Problem 5: one unit in many tables

This is the opposite problem,
where the same kind of observation is split across many files,
for example one file per year or one file per hospital site.
If the files have the same columns,
we can stack them together with `bind_rows()`,
or give `read_csv()` all the file names at once.

## How hospitals store data

Hospital databases follow the paper's third rule.
Each kind of observational unit gets its own table,
and the tables are linked together by ID columns.

- `patients` has one row per patient
- `encounters` has one row per visit, with the patient's ID
- `conditions`, `medications`, and `observations` have one row per record,
  with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.

[Synthea](https://synthetichealth.github.io/synthea/) creates fake,
but realistic, patient records that are stored this way.
Its [downloads page](https://synthetichealth.github.io/downloads.html)
has samples of 100 patients as CSV files,
and in the HL7 FHIR and C-CDA formats.

## Beyond CSVs: health data standards

In practice, health data usually doesn't come to us as a folder of CSV files.
It's stored and shared using data standards.

- [HL7](https://www.hl7.org/) is the family of standards
  hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
- [FHIR](https://hl7.org/fhir/) (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources)
  is HL7's newer standard,
  where data like a patient, an encounter, or an observation
  is sent as a "resource" through web APIs
- The [OMOP Common Data Model](https://ohdsi.github.io/CommonDataModel/),
  from the [OHDSI](https://www.ohdsi.org/) community,
  is a shared database layout for observational health data,
  so the same analysis code can run on databases from many hospitals

All of these follow the same idea as the paper's third rule,
with one table (or resource) for each kind of observational unit,
linked together by IDs.
